newsitem.title: LITHUANIA: Key Lithuanian bank seeks investors as recovers.
newsitem.headline: Key Lithuanian bank seeks investors as recovers.

text.p: Lithuania's Litimpeks Bank, formerly a leading bank but now recovering after being shut down, said on Tuesday it was hoping to entice foreign investors with a new 20 million litas share issue.
But it conceded that the going will be tough as it aims to restore its credibility following the closure, which was part of a wider banking crisis in the Baltic state.
"We hope to interest foreigners in our stock issue of 20 million litas which will be on the market until March 31, 1997," Litimpeks vice-president Jonas Bobelis told Reuters.
"Our main problem is restoring our reputation. Our credibility took a hit last year," he added.
The closure of Litimpeks along with what was the largest bank, Innovation Bank, caused a severe crisis in the whole banking system, from which it is just recovering.
The government had to restructure the sector, shutting down some banks for good and bailing out others.
Litimpeks was reopened in June without the support of government cash and Bobelis said the bank was now talking to foreign investors as it rebuilds itself.
"We are talking to American, Korean and other Baltic banks," he said but would not name specific investors.
Litimpeks previously had talks with Poland's Kredyt Bank but it decided to open its own branch office.
Bobelis also said Litimpeks has had talks with the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development (EBRD), which has taken stakes in other Baltic banks.
The bank's share capital now stands at 39.5 million litas and its profit for the first nine months was 258,000 litas.
Its assets at the end of September were 211.2 million litas, making it the fifth largest commercial bank.
But deposits are still below previous levels, falling from 198.2 million litas at the end of December 1995 to 150.3 million litas at the end of September 1996.
Bobelis said that Litimpeks was also considering an issue of global depository receipts (GDR), one of which has already been carried out by leading bank, Vilnius Bank.
Litimpeks said its capital adequacy ratio met the minimum 13 percent required by the central bank.
"We have been restructuring, tightening our belts and shedding assets and staff," Bobelis said.
